bridge: Builds on P05 tests, M04 probability, B03 APIs and S01 threat modelling. This is an AI-system security bridge; neural-network training and calculus are not prerequisites for its paper exercises.
teaching:
Machine learning fits parameters from data; inference uses the fitted model on an input. A language model predicts tokens under its learned/contextual distribution. Tokens are representation units rather than a fixed number of characters. A plausible continuation is not an independently verified fact, permission grant or database query result.

Separate model weights, application instructions, retrieved data and tools. Prompting supplies context without ordinarily retraining weights. Fine-tuning changes parameters. Retrieval supplies selected documents at inference time. An embedding is a numerical representation used for similarity; closeness does not establish ownership or truth. A tool is application code that can read or act outside the model.

Security analysis follows assets and authority through this pipeline. Which user may retrieve which documents? What reaches the provider? Who validates proposed actions? Keep ordinary server-side controls outside probabilistic decisions. The required exercises use fixed records and mock proposals, so they require no account, model download, paid API or live scoring run.

A parameter is a learned weight; a hyperparameter is a design/training setting such as a learning rate. They are not synonyms. A decoder-only transformer can predict successive tokens without a separate encoder. Encoder-only and encoder–decoder designs serve other tasks. A token may be a word, word piece, punctuation or another unit; the video uses words to simplify the picture.

Pretraining adjusts weights using a prediction objective. Post-training can use supervised instruction examples, preference methods or reinforcement learning; RLHF is one route rather than a universal stage. Ordinary inference uses the trained model and its current context; adding a prompt or retrieving a document does not by itself update its stored weights. The probability of the next token concerns the model’s continuation distribution, not the truth, safety or authorisation of the resulting statement. Domain expertise and source checking remain necessary.

Known input positions can often be processed in parallel, but an autoregressive generated token depends on earlier generated tokens. A fast or fluent response is not evidence that the application checked a permission. Keep a model’s proposed action separate from the code that validates identity, resource scope and approval before executing it.
example:
Fictional assistant pipeline
User A asks: summarise my note.
Application authenticates A -> retrieves A-owned note1.
Model receives task + allowed note text -> proposes a summary.
Application displays summary as text.
No send_email or delete_file tool exists.
Assets: note contents, session, model/provider logs.
Authority: application ACL, never model-generated owner field.
explanation: A model can summarise an allowed document without receiving a credential or authority to read every account. A wrong summary is a quality problem; exposing B's note is an access-control problem. They can coexist and need different checks.
exercise: Draw the supplied pipeline with trust boundaries. Classify these changes: passing B's note to A; adding a delete tool; fine-tuning on notes; retrieving an extra public document. Identify changed data/authority assumptions.
solution: B's note is an unauthorised disclosure before generation. A delete tool adds action authority. Fine-tuning changes model-data retention/parameter risks. A public document adds an untrusted content source even if it contains no private data.
challenge: Explain training, inference, prompting, retrieval, embeddings and tool execution in your own words. Design a read-only note assistant and list three security checks enforced by application code rather than by asking the model to behave.
challenge_solution: Authenticate caller; filter retrieval by owner before model exposure; render output safely and provide no write/send capability. State provider data policy and logging assumptions. This bridge supports security engineering, not a claim of full ML-theory competence.
